title: Alkaline Phosphatase in Clinical Practice
subject: Pathology
summary: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is an enzyme from liver, bone and other tissues. Elevated ALP signals hepatobiliary or bone disease; interpretation depends on clinical context and accompanying labs.

sections.p: ALP is a membrane‑bound enzyme released into serum from liver, bile ducts, bone, placenta and gut. It is measured by a colorimetric assay; normal adult range is ≤200 IU/dL.
b: High ALP = liver/biliary or bone pathology until proven otherwise
Low ALP is rare, seen in severe malnutrition or hypophosphatasia

sections.p: ALP itself is not staged, but the underlying disease is. Use disease‑specific scores (e.g., Child‑Pugh for cholestasis, WHO criteria for bone metastases).
b: Mild: 200‑400 IU/dL, often asymptomatic
Moderate: 400‑800 IU/dL, may have jaundice or bone pain
Severe: >800 IU/dL, suggests obstructive jaundice, extensive bone disease or infiltrative liver disease

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, common causes are grouped by organ system.
b: Liver/biliary: viral hepatitis B/C, obstructive gallstone disease, schistosomal peri‑portal fibrosis, HIV‑related cholangiopathy
Bone: vitamin D deficiency rickets/osteomalacia, sickle‑cell bone infarcts, Paget disease (rare), metastatic prostate or breast cancer
Pregnancy/placenta: third‑trimester physiological rise
Gut: intestinal infection with severe diarrhoea (minor rise)
Medications/herbals: traditional remedies containing phosphates, antiepileptics (e.g., phenytoin) causing bone turnover

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic, or present with signs related to the source organ.
b: Liver: jaundice, pruritus, right upper quadrant pain, dark urine
Bone: bone pain, fractures, bowing of legs in children, muscle weakness
Systemic: fatigue, weight loss, fever in infection

sections.p: When imaging is unavailable, rely on clinical pattern and basic labs; consider referral for ultrasound if possible.

t.b: Is the enzyme elevated? – Confirms a biochemical abnormality; magnitude guides urgency
Is the source hepatic? – High GGT with high ALP points to liver/biliary origin; normal GGT suggests bone

t.a: Serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, 25‑OH vitamin D
t.b: Are bone metabolism abnormalities present? – Low calcium/phosphate with high ALP suggests vitamin D deficiency or rickets

t.a: Liver function panel (ALT, AST, bilirubin, albumin)
t.b: Is there concurrent hepatocellular injury? – Isolated ALP rise with normal transaminases favors cholestasis

t.a: Abdominal ultrasound (or bedside ultrasound if CT unavailable)
t.b: Is there biliary obstruction or liver lesion? – Detects gallstones, dilated ducts, focal masses

t.a: X‑ray of affected bones or bedside radiograph
t.b: Is there bone disease? – Shows looser zones, fractures, Paget changes

t.a: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) if leukocytosis present
t.b: Is leukocytosis reactive? – High LAP suggests leukemoid reaction; low LAP raises suspicion for CML (rare locally)

sections.p: Unchecked cholestasis can lead to cirrhosis; severe bone disease can cause pathological fractures.
b: Progressive jaundice, encephalopathy → urgent hepatology referral
Severe bone pain with deformities → risk of fractures, need orthopedic input
Persistent ALP >800 IU/dL without explanation → consider malignancy

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause; supportive measures address symptoms and prevent complications.
b: Viral hepatitis: antiviral therapy (e.g., tenofovir for HBV) – reduces hepatic inflammation
Obstructive biliary disease: endoscopic stone removal or surgical drainage – relieves cholestasis
Vitamin D deficiency rickets: high‑dose vitamin D3 and calcium supplementation – normalises bone turnover
Sickle‑cell bone crisis: analgesia, hydration, transfusion if severe – lowers bone ALP
Avoid drugs that further raise ALP without indication (e.g., unnecessary phenytoin) – prevents iatrogenic bone loss

sections.p: Repeat ALP and relevant panels after 4‑6 weeks of therapy to gauge response.
b: Monitor GGT and bilirubin for liver disease resolution
Check calcium, phosphate, vitamin D for bone recovery
Educate patients on safe herbal use and nutrition

sections.p: Other enzymes or conditions that raise similar labs.
b: Gamma‑glutamyl transferase – also rises in cholestasis but not in bone disease
Serum aminotransferases – indicate hepatocellular injury, not cholestasis
Serum creatine kinase – rises in muscle injury, not liver/bone
High ALP with normal GGT may still be hepatic if GGT assay unavailable
Pregnancy‑related ALP rise can be mistaken for pathology
Hemolysis or sample mishandling can falsely elevate ALP

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive jaundice, altered mental status, or coagulopathy
Severe bone pain with inability to bear weight

faq.q: Why is GGT measured with ALP?
faq.a: GGT helps differentiate hepatic from bone sources; both rise in cholestasis, only bone ALP rises alone.
Severe malaria may mildly raise ALP via hepatic involvement, but marked elevations usually point to other causes.

faq.q: Is a high ALP always dangerous?
faq.a: Not alone; the danger lies in the underlying disease. Mild, isolated rises often need observation rather than urgent treatment.

exam: A 35‑year‑old man with sickle‑cell disease presents with leg pain and ALP 650 IU/dL. – Identify the likely source, required investigations, and immediate management steps.
A pregnant woman in her third trimester has ALP 300 IU/dL, normal GGT, and mild pruritus. – Explain why this is physiologic and when to investigate further.
A child with rickets has ALP 900 IU/dL, low calcium, low phosphate, and low vitamin D. – Outline the treatment hierarchy and monitoring plan.
A patient with known hepatitis B shows ALP 750 IU/dL, bilirubin 5 mg/dL, and GGT 200 IU/L. – Discuss the significance, next diagnostic test, and urgency of referral.
In a rural clinic, only ALP and bilirubin are available. ALP is 850 IU/dL, bilirubin normal. – How would you decide if the problem is hepatic or bone without GGT?
A 60‑year‑old man with weight loss has ALP 1200 IU/dL, normal calcium, and normal GGT. – What red‑flag diagnoses must you consider and what imaging would you request?
Why is leukocyte alkaline phosphatase useful in a patient with high white count and elevated ALP? – Explain interpretation and clinical impact.
A patient on long‑term phenytoin develops ALP 500 IU/dL. – Discuss why the drug may be responsible and alternative anticonvulsants.
